items.title: The fighters are a tiny diorama in the middle band; a huge empty blurred void owns the top 30% of the screen
items.what: In the in-fight screenshots (3, 4, 11, 14) the two fighters span only from roughly 37% to 62% of the screen height — their heads sit below the halfway line and each body is about 300px tall in a 1280px-tall frame. Above them, from just under the HUD bar down to the shoji windows (roughly y=150–430) there is nothing but out-of-focus brown backdrop: no banners, no crowd, no readable detail, just smear and a few dust motes. Below, the legend panel plus the two dials eat the bottom 33%. The net result is a ~10%-of-screen action zone sandwiched between two dead zones. The same framing is reused for the intro card and the IPPON moment, which is why the 'IPPON / HASANABI / SPINNING BACK KICK' title in screenshot 12 floats 250px above the actual kick.
items.why: This is the first thing a player sees and it kills the fight's presence. Photoreal sprite fighters are the most expensive asset in the build and they're rendered at thumbnail size, so faces, gi detail, and limb silhouettes — the entire reason to use photoreal art — are unreadable on a 390px-wide phone. At this scale a spinning back kick and a reverse punch look almost identical, which also hurts read-and-react play.
items.how: Push the camera in / narrow FOV so the fighter pair fills from about 28% to 72% of the portrait height (roughly 1.5x their current on-screen height), with the mat horizon landing just above the legend panel and the shoji band cropped to a thin strip behind their heads. Anchor the camera so the pair stays centered as they separate (dolly + clamp, don't zoom out past ~1.2x). Then move the floating text into the space it earns: the IPPON banner and move-name toast should sit just above the fighters' heads (~22–28% height), not at 25% of an empty frame.

items.title: The fighters read as flat cutouts pasted on a photo — they are not in the dojo's light
items.what: Everything in the scene is amber/tungsten, but the white gi in screenshots 3, 4, 9 and 14 is near-neutral bright white (it is the brightest thing on screen outside the HUD), with the same flat frontal lighting on both fighters regardless of the stage-left volumetric shaft. Their edges are pin-sharp while the backdrop two metres behind them is heavily bokeh'd, and grounding is a single wide, uniformly soft brown smudge under each body — in screenshot 4 you can see mat lines running straight through where the shadow should be dense under the rear foot. The landscape shot (9) makes it worst: two crisp, cool-white, hard-edged bodies on a soft warm plate.
items.why: It reads as a sticker-on-background mobile knockoff instead of the cinematic dojo the rest of the pipeline is paying for. It also breaks spatial read: with no per-foot contact shadow the players can't tell how far apart the fighters actually are, which matters in a game where range decides whether a lunge punch connects.
items.how: Three cheap passes on the sprite draw: (1) multiply the sprite by the scene key-light color and add a warm rim term from the stage-left light direction so the gi lands around #EBDCC2 instead of #F2F0EC, and let the split-tone/vignette/grain apply to the sprites too (render them before post, not as a UI layer); (2) replace the single blob with two small hard-core contact ellipses (one per foot, ~60% opacity, 8px blur) under a larger soft ambient occluder, and dim the mat texture beneath them; (3) add 0.5–1px of edge softening / a touch of the same DOF blur radius used on the backdrop so the silhouette doesn't cut like a die-cut sticker.

items.title: Scoring a point has no visual impact at the point of contact — only a text banner
items.what: Screenshot 12 and 15 are the IPPON frames. At the actual contact — red's shin against white's chest, white's fist against red's ribs — there is nothing: no flash, no spark, no dust puff, no compression of the sprites, just a tiny yellow tick mark. All the feedback lives as a typographic banner ('IPPON / ASMONGOLD / STEPPING LUNGE PUNCH') sitting 250px above the bodies, and the score in the top HUD flips from 0 to 1 with no emphasis, no pip animation, no color pulse. Screenshot 5 is the same problem earlier in the chain: the label 'LUNGE PUNCH' appears while both fighters are still in the identical idle stance as screenshots 3/4, so the only evidence that the input registered is a word near the top of the screen.
items.why: In point karate the whole game is 'did that one contact count'. Right now the player has to read text to find out, in the part of the screen their eyes are not on, while their thumbs are at the bottom. The bout ends (screenshot 8, 0–2½) without the player ever having felt a hit land. That is the single biggest reason a fighting game feels cheap.
items.how: Build a 250–350ms impact beat fired at the contact frame: (1) 3-frame hitstop on both sprites; (2) a small additive radial flash + 6–10 dust/sweat particles spawned at the contact world position, scaled by half-point vs full-point; (3) 4–6px camera shake plus a quick 1.05x punch-in; (4) the point pip spawns at the contact point and flies to that fighter's number in the top HUD, where the number scales 1.3x and pulses amber (white) / red (Hasan); (5) a 30ms + 60ms haptic double tap. Keep the IPPON word, but drop it right above the fighters' heads so flash, pose, and text are one glance.

items.title: The two dials are visual twins; the only difference is a 6px dot, and the active-drag ring draws outside the pad
items.what: In every fight screenshot the left and right dials are pixel-identical rings — same diameter, same rim color, same four chevrons, same brown gradient knob. The only differentiators are a tiny center dot (blue vs amber, ~6px) and the words STANCE / TECHNIQUE in 10px letter-spaced gray below the pads, i.e. below the thumbs that cover them. Above them a permanent 90px legend slab ('◄ step ▲ jump / ► step ▼ crouch' | '◄ back ► forward / ▲ up ▼ down') eats stage height and still doesn't say what any *pair* does. Worse, in screenshot 5 the active technique input draws a large white circle that breaks out past the dial's own outer rim to the upper-right, overlapping the pad border and the chevron — it looks like a rendering bug, not a state.
items.why: The entire move set is stance-direction plus technique-direction, so grabbing the wrong dial means a wrong move in a game where one clean contact ends the exchange. With identical pads and labels hidden under the thumb, players will mis-grab constantly in the first bout — and the 20-entry Techniques list (screenshot 6) means they already have a lot to hold in their heads.
items.how: Color-code the whole control, not the dot: cool steel-blue rim, chevrons and knob for STANCE; amber/ember rim and knob for TECHNIQUE, and print the label inside the ring's top arc so a thumb on the knob doesn't hide it. Clamp the drag indicator to the pad radius (inset 4px) so it can never exit the rim. Then replace the static legend slab with a live combo readout: as soon as one dial is held, show the resulting move name and its value ('STEPPING LUNGE PUNCH · mid · full point') in a single centered chip directly above the pads, so the move list teaches itself during play.

items.title: The pre-boot progress bar never shows any fill — the first screen looks hung
items.what: Screenshot 1: the bar under 'Downloading the game' is one flat uniform brown track running nearly edge to edge (x≈37 to x≈555) with no filled segment, no indeterminate sweep, no percentage, and no byte/step count. Above it, 'Downloading the game' is a generic sentence. The rest of the frame is ~300px of empty black above the logo and ~420px of empty black below the 'A SHOEMONEY AI LABS GAME' line, and the logo carries a hard offset black matte behind the blue S that reads as an unmasked PNG shadow rather than a designed drop shadow.
items.why: This is a WebGPU browser game with a heavy download: the loading screen is where bounce happens. A bar with zero fill for several seconds is indistinguishable from a frozen page, so players close the tab before they ever see the dojo. It's also the branded first impression for ShoeMoney.
items.how: Drive the fill from actual fetch progress (sum of expected asset bytes; fall back to a per-asset step count) and render a real amber fill with a 1px warm highlight, plus a right-aligned '43%' and a step label ('Fighters', 'Dojo', 'Shaders'). Add a slow indeterminate shimmer on the track so it is never static even at 0%. Tighten the layout: move the logo/title/bar block up so it is optically centered around 45% height, and soften or re-render the logo's black matte as a true blurred shadow at ~40% opacity.
